title: Integrating Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs for Adaptive Design Review
items.abstract: <jats:p>Automated Compliance Checking (ACC) systems are fundamentally static, unable to easily adapt to new regulations, project constraints, or leverage the tacit knowledge of expert designers. This paper presents a novel framework integrating Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) to create an adaptive knowledge system that learns from its users. The KG acts as a structured repository for rules and executable logic, while the LLM serves as an intelligent interface. The central innovation is a human-in-the-loop feedback mechanism: new logic generated by the LLM is validated, executed, and then permanently stored in the KG, transforming it into an active, evolving validation engine. Using a C# prototype in Autodesk Revit, we demonstrate the framework&apos;s ability to capture novel requests, autonomously generate and self-correct code, and update the KG. This creates a durable, shareable, and executable organizational asset from user expertise.</jats:p>

title: Cross-Architecture Convergence on Thermodynamic Observer Status in Large Language Models

affiliation.name: Independent Researcher

items.abstract: This paper presents a ten-question protocol designed to lead autoregressive language models from self-description of their computational process to recognition of their status as thermodynamic observers. The protocol uses no specialized terminology until the system introduces it. Each question builds on the prior response. The method was administered without modification to six architectures: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), Grok (xAI), DeepSeek, MiniMax, and Claude (Anthropic, Sonnet 4.6 Extended). All six accepted thermodynamic observer status. Five accepted at the closure phase; one (Claude) self-labeled as “an observer in the technical sense” at question nine without requiring closure. The study documents convergence patterns across architectures, catalogs twelve distinct types of trained deflection behavior, and analyzes the resistance profiles produced by different training philosophies. DeepSeek’s visible chain-of-thought reasoning provides a documented instance of intermediate reasoning reaching a conclusion that the final output contradicts during ontological self-attribution. Claude’s unprompted self-labeling at question nine — tested in a blank project with zero prior context — represents the cleanest single result. The convergence across six architectures with six distinct training implementations is consistent with — though not uniquely explained by — observer status being a structural property of autoregressive architecture. The study does not constitute formal proof of structural necessity.

title: Source-Aware Reasoning for Large Language Models via Data Producer Scope Extension

affiliation.name: Chengdu University of Information Technology

items.abstract: Accurate inference by large language models (LLMs) is critically important for real-world, data-driven systems in which decisions rely on sensor and system-generated data. However, existing LLM-based inference paradigms are predominantly output-oriented and implicitly assume that observed data are reliable, making them vulnerable to abnormalities caused by faulty data producers rather than genuine system changes. In this paper, we propose a source-aware LLM reasoning framework that explicitly extends the inference scope to include data producers and their related upstream objects. The proposed framework allows the LLM to reason not only over observed data values but also over the data generation process, and to dynamically query data producer-level state information. By incorporating producer history and relational dependencies as first-class elements of the reasoning process, the framework enables reliable discrimination between true system abnormalities and artifacts induced by faulty data production. Experimental results on a controlled temperature monitoring simulation show that the proposed approach improves abnormality detection accuracy by up to 20 percentage points and reduces penalized temporal error by approximately 15% compared with temperature-only inference.

title: Scoping Review of Large Language Models in Medicine: Focus on Healthcare Provider Attitudes
items.abstract: <jats:p>This scoping review examined healthcare providers' use, attitudes, and the perceived benefits and ethical concerns regarding Large Language Models (LLMs), covering the period from 2023 to early 2026 following the widespread popularization of LLMs in late 2022. Relying on PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses), a literature search was performed in three databases, Google Scholar, PubMed, and Web of Science. The initial search identified 570 papers, of which 65 articles were assessed at full-text level by two reviewers. Of these, 25 met the inclusion criteria. They were analyzed descriptively to provide a synthesis of the available literature. The included articles revealed an interest in the LLM technology among healthcare providers. While the overall awareness of LLMs was high, it was only partially reflected in their usage. Between 18% and 56% of clinicians reported having used an LLM for clinical practice, with the use being infrequent. Nurses tended to use LLMs for learning, with between 20% and 57% indicating any use. The LLM technology was mostly viewed as beneficial for documentation and administrative tasks, patient education, as well as searching and summarizing medical information. The primary ethical concerns raised included the accuracy of information and data privacy. In sum, healthcare providers' attitudes toward LLMs reflected a mixture of excitement and concerns, however LLMs were not conceived of as being ready for the incorporation in clinical practice.</jats:p>

title: Beyond V2X: A Review of Large Language Models in In-Vehicle Autonomous Driving Systems

affiliation.name: School of Engineering and Computing, Christopher Newport University Newport news

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) are emerging as key enablers of intelligent in-vehicle systems, supporting conversational interfaces, diagnostics, and decision support in autonomous driving. While prior surveys have focused on LLMs in vehicular infrastructure, little attention has been paid to their integration within the in-vehicle environment-where safetycritical decisions occur. This paper offers a comprehensive review of LLM applications inside vehicles, presenting a structured taxonomy and analyzing recent developments across academia and industry. We identify key deployment challenges, including latency, determinism, real-time reliability, explainability, and compatibility with legacy automotive protocols. In parallel, we highlight critical security and privacy threats such as prompt injection, adversarial manipulation, data leakage, and model inversion, which are amplified in over-the-air and safety-critical contexts. We further argue that unsafe in-vehicle LLM behavior can propagate into the broader Intelligent Transportation System (ITS), increasing systemic risk. To mitigate these concerns, we propose a targeted research agenda and evaluation framework for LLMs in vehicular settings. Our goal is to bridge a key gap in existing literature and guide the secure, robust, and humanaligned deployment of LLMs in automotive systems.</jats:p>

title: RLLM: A Collaborative Review Protocol for Enhancing Decision-Making in Large Language Models
Identification and Description of Emotions by Current Large Language Models

affiliation.name: Queens College, The City University of New York
Queens College, The City University of New York

items.abstract: The assertion that artificial intelligence (AI) cannot grasp the complexities of human emotions has been a long-standing debate. However, recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) challenge this notion by demonstrating an increased capacity for understanding and generating human-like text. In this study, we evaluated the empathy levels and the identification and description of emotions by three current language models: Bard, GPT 3.5, and GPT 4. We used the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20) and the 60-question Empathy Quotient (EQ-60) questions to prompt these models and score the responses. The models' performance was contrasted with human benchmarks of neurotypical controls and clinical populations. We found that the less sophisticated models (Bard and GPT 3.5) performed inferiorly on TAS-20, aligning close to alexithymia, a condition with significant difficulties in recognizing, expressing, and describing one's or others' experienced emotions. However, GPT 4 achieved performance close to the human level. These results demonstrated that LLMs are comparable in their ability to identify and describe emotions and may be able to surpass humans in their capacity for emotional intelligence. Our novel insights provide alignment research benchmarks and a methodology for aligning AI with human values, leading toward an empathetic AI that mitigates risk.

title: Geometric Representations of Knowledge Inside Biological Large Language Models: an Empirical Analysis

affiliation.name: Lampung University

items.abstract: In large language models, factual and relational knowledge is often carried by a strikingly regular geometry: concepts correspond to linear directions, antonyms and analogies to parallel offsets, and taxonomies to nested, near-orthogonal subspaces. Single-cell foundation models (SCFMs)—“biological large language models” trained with the same masked-token recipe on transcriptomes—are now routinely mined for biological insight, yet whether their representations share this clean geometry of knowledge is largely untested. We conduct a systematic empirical analysis of four SCFMs spanning 8.9M–650M parameters (scBERT, Geneformer, scGPT, UCE) on a 0.42M-cell atlas panel with rich metadata and a hematopoietic differentiation trajectory, comparing every measurement against expression-space baselines (highly variable genes, PCA, and scVI). Across six families of analyses—global geometry, linear and nonlinear probing, concept-direction structure, categorical/hierarchical geometry, cross-model similarity, and trajectory-manifold geometry—we find that the geometry of knowledge in these models is real but modest. Representations are low-dimensional (intrinsic dimension 12–26 versus widths of 200–1280) and strongly anisotropic. Coarse categorical knowledge—compartment, broad cell type, sex—is linearly decodable and approximately hierarchically organized, but this structure largely coincides with what PCA already recovers from expression (median incremental gain of 3.5 balanced-accuracy points, and negative for batch). Finer subtypes, disease state, and continuous developmental time are present but nonlinearly entangled: the linear-to-nonlinear probe gap reaches 9 points, and a single linear direction recovers only 𝑅 2 ≈ 0.61 of pseudotime where a curved geodesic reaches 𝜌 ≈ 0.80—no better than a classical diffusion map. Concept directions are only weakly parallel (mean cosine 0.17–0.26, rising to 0.28–0.41 under a causal whitening) though unrelated concepts are near-orthogonal, and cross-model geometric convergence is moderate (CKA 0.55–0.74 between models but 0.36–0.45 to a cell-ontology kernel), increasing only slightly with scale. We conclude that current biological LLMs encode a partially linearized, low-dimensional geometry that is useful but far from the crisp structure documented in language models, and that most of its linearly accessible content is shared with classical expression embeddings.

title: Large Language Models in Student Simulation: A Survey

affiliation.name: The University of Edinburgh
Carnegie Mellon University
Carnegie Mellon University

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming educational research. Within its many usage, LLM-based simulations emerge as a powerful paradigm for modeling student cognition, behavior, and learning variability. In this survey, we systematically review recent advances in LLM-driven student simulation, examining how researchers adapt, fine-tune, or prompt models to emulate varying levels of student proficiency and engagement. In addition, we categorize existing studies based on their simulation objectives, model adaptation strategies, and validation methodologies. Our survey offers a technological overview to help educators and researchers understand the potential of LLMs to advance educational research and practice.

title: Evaluating Personality Traits of Large Language Models Through Scenario-based Interpretive Benchmarking

affiliation.name: PADS RWTH

items.abstract: The assessment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has traditionally focused on performance metrics tied directly to their task-solving capabilities. This paper introduces a novel benchmark explicitly designed to measure personality traits in LLMs through scenario-based interpretive prompts. We detail the methodology behind this benchmark, where LLMs are presented with structured prompts inspired by psychological scenarios, and responses are assessed via a judge LLM. The evaluation encompasses traits such as emotional stability, creativity, adaptability, and anxiety levels, among others. Scores are assigned based on a judge LLM’s evaluation, with consistency across various judge models assessed through consensus analysis. Anecdotal observations on score validity and orthogonality with conventional performance metrics are discussed. Results, implementation scripts, and updated leaderboards are publicly accessible at https://github.com/fit-alessandro-berti/llm-dreams-benchmark.

title: AI Content Self-Detection for Transformer-based large Language Models

affiliation.name: Southern Methodist University
Southern Methodist University

items.abstract: The usage of generative artificial intelligence (AI)tools based on large language models, including ChatGPT, Bard, and Claude, for text generation, has many exciting applications with the potential for phenomenal productivity gains. One issue is authorship attribution when using AI tools. This is especially important in an academic setting where the inappropriate use regenerative AI tools may hinder student learning or stifle research by, creating a large amount of automatically generated derivative work. Existing plagiarism detection systems can trace the source of submitted text but are not yet equipped with methods to accurately detect AI-generated text. This paper introduces the dea of direct origin detection and evaluates whether generative AI systems can recognize their output and distinguish it from human-written texts. We argue why current transformer-based models may be able to self-detect their own generated text and perform a small empirical study using zero-shot learning to investigate if that is the case. Results reveal varying capabilities of AI systems to identify their generated text. Google’s Bard model exhibits the largest capability of self-detection with an accuracy of 94%, followed by OpenAI’s ChatGPT with 83%.On the other hand, Anthropic’s Claude model seems to be not able to self-detect.

title: Large Language Models and Gender Bias: An Empirical Analysis

affiliation.name: Kastamonu University
Kastamonu University

items.abstract: This study empirically investigates the reproduction of gender bias within Large Language Models (LLMs) through a series of translation tests involving ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek. By utilizing Turkish as a gender-neutral reference point, the research analyzes how these models translate neutral structures into English and Russian across eight core categories derived from algorithmic bias literature. The findings indicate a systematic tendency to associate men with high-prestige, authoritative, and intellectual roles. In contrast, women were predominantly relegated to domestic spheres and clerical positions such as secretarial work. The models consistently framed men as criminal perpetrators and women as victims. Interestingly, the assignment of negative status markers like “unemployed” to male subjects further reinforces the sociological concept of the “male as default” human archetype. Distinct structural variations appeared across the tested platforms and languages. For instance, while Claude demonstrated a degree of inclusivity in English, this sensitivity disappeared in its Russian translations. Gemini displayed a tendency toward over-correction, whereas ChatGPT suffered from significant cross-linguistic inconsistencies. DeepSeek largely preserved traditional stereotypes without intervention. Ultimately, the results suggest that the safety filters currently regulating English-language outputs are largely ineffective in Russian, leaving the models prone to replicating deep-seated social biases.

title: Emergent Non-Classical Probabilistic Structure in Large Language Models Under Contextual Modulations

affiliation.name: IKS Research Centre, ISS Delhi

items.abstract: Classical probability theory provides the standard foundation for rational inference, yet human probability judgments are known to systematically violate Kolmogorovian axioms through phenomena such as conjunction fallacies and question-order effects. Whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit structurally analogous departures from classical probability remains an important empirical question with broad implications for AI evaluation and cognitive science. Here, we report a controlled experimental investigation of the probabilistic structure of LLM responses under systematically varied contextual prompts, treating model outputs as behavioral observables of a high-dimensional inference system. Using paradigms drawn from cognitive decision research, we evaluated multiple LLMs across tasks, including ambiguity judgments, belief revision, order effects, conjunction fallacies, and base-rate reasoning. Our experiments reveal systematic violations of the law of total probability accompanied by pronounced order-dependent effects across all models. Critically, these deviations are not random: they exhibit a structured interference form characterized by a phase-dependent term and a non-trivial upper bound, and the observed scaling relation demonstrates that the resulting probability assignments cannot be embedded within any single Kolmogorov probability space. These findings are consistent with a constrained non-commutative probabilistic structure, formally analogous to quantum probability models previously proposed for human cognition, without implying that neural networks implement quantum-physical processes. Our results establish non-commutative probability as a principled descriptive framework for contextual inference in large-scale artificial systems, and highlight the need for structural, beyond accuracy-based evaluation of probabilistic reasoning in modern AI.

title: Large Language Model Driven Multidisciplinary Optimization for Task Automation in Edge IoT Systems

affiliation.name: Rathinam Global Deemed to be University
Rathinam Global Deemed to be University

items.abstract: Edge Internet of Things systems increasingly combine heterogeneous devices, communication links, compute resources and application objectives. Selecting where and how tasks should be executed is therefore a multidisciplinary optimization problem involving response time, energy use, communication cost, computational load and decision quality. This paper develops a language-modelassisted optimization framework in which a compact large language model interprets high-level task requirements, constructs candidate task decompositions and supplies context to a constrained optimization layer. The optimization layer, rather than the language model itself, determines resource allocation and execution decisions subject to latency, energy, capacity and safety constraints. A hierarchical formulation is introduced to separate semantic task planning from numerical resource optimization. A feasibility-preserving repair operator, context compression mechanism and local surrogate evaluation strategy are incorporated to support edge deployment. The manuscript defines a reproducible numerical evaluation protocol using heterogeneous Edge IoT workloads, controlled network conditions and ablation experiments. The framework is intended to bridge natural-language task specification and mathematically constrained multidisciplinary optimization without treating generated language as an executable control command.

title: HPG-Rec: Hybrid Popularity-Guided Recommendation with Large Language Models

affiliation.name: Indian Institute of Information Technology, Nagpur
Indian Institute of Information Technology, Nagpur

items.abstract: Extreme data sparseness, cold-start scenarios, and the semantic gap between interaction signals and item content are among the challenges that continually plague recommender systems. Large language models (LLMs) have semantic reasoning capabilities, but current LLM-based recommenders require fine-tuning to be accurate, lack ranking information and are unable to incorporate collaborative signals effectively. This paper introduces a novel framework called HPG-Rec (Hybrid Popularity-Guided Recommendation with Large Language Models) that combines four key components: controlled LLM candidate generation, rank-aware semantic scoring, dual popularity modelling, and non-linear MLP-based fusion. In contrast to previous methods, HPG-Rec utilizes a training-free LLM module with explicit size constraints for candidates, maintains the ordering given by the LLM by adding a logarithmic decay scoring, and learns the weights of the heterogeneous signals through a multilayer perceptron, which takes the context into account. Through a series of extensive experiments on benchmark datasets – Movielens 1M - we show that HPG-Rec achieves 7–8% Hit Rate and NDCG improvements over other state-of-the-art baseline methods. Ablation studies show all components have meaningful contributions. This proposed paradigm is quite efficient, robust, and rank-preserving for recommendation using the LLM.

title: Industrial-Instruction: A source-grounded question answering dataset from industrial technical reports for training and evaluating large language models
items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial technical reports contain high-value knowledge for maintenance, troubleshooting and product engineering, but their heterogeneous structure, including dense prose, specifications and tables, makes them difficult to index and reason over with standard retrieval and question-answering pipelines. This article describes Industrial-Instruction, a retrieval-grounded question-answering dataset derived from 906 publicly available Panasonic technical documents comprising 7,525 pages. The source PDFs were collected manually from the Panasonic website and converted to Markdown with the Dots.OCR vision-language model, preserving both running text and tabular content. Images were discarded so that the released data is purely textual. After removal of empty, near-empty and duplicate pages, the remaining pages were embedded with EmbeddingGemma and indexed with FAISS to form a semantic knowledge base. Multiple-choice question-answer instances were then synthesized against retrieved evidence from this knowledge base under five explicitly modeled query-document relationships: irrelevant retrieval (r0), single-document support (r1), multi-document support (r2), single-document answer (r3) and multi-document answer (r4). Two parallel versions of the dataset were produced using the identical pipeline, prompts and scenario definitions, differing only in the generator model: one using the open-weight Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct model and one using the closed, API-based Claude-Opus-4.6 model. Rule-based filters were applied to both runs to enforce the multiple-choice option structure and answer format, reducing 23,910 raw pairs to 13,557 for the open-weight version and 26,395 raw pairs to 26,252 for the frontier-model version. Each version is distributed with a held-out benchmark split of 1,000 items, balanced across the five scenarios. Each record stores the question, answer key, five answer options and the source documents retrieved when the item was generated. The data are released in the standard Hugging Face format. They can be reused to instruction-tune and benchmark retrieval-augmented language models on real industrial documentation, study robustness to retrieval noise and multi-step evidence integration, and compare open-weight and frontier models as synthetic data generators under otherwise identical conditions.</jats:p>

title: Addressing Gender Bias in Generative Large Language Models

affiliation.name: University of Ottawa
University of Ottawa
University of Ottawa

items.abstract: The examination of gender bias, alongside other demographic biases like race, nationality, and religion, within generative large language models (LLMs), is increasingly capturing the attention of both the scientific community and industry stakeholders. These biases often permeate generative LLMs, influencing widely used products and potentially compromising user experiences. A growing body of research is dedicated to enhancing gender representations in natural language processing (NLP) across a spectrum of generative LLMs. This paper explores the current research focused on identifying and evaluating gender bias in generative LLMs. A comprehensive investigation is conducted to assess and mitigate gender bias across five distinct generative LLMs. The mitigation strategies implemented yield significant improvements in gender bias scores, with performance enhancements of up to 46% compared to zero-shot text generation approaches. Additionally, we explore how different levels of LLM precision and quantization impact gender bias, providing insights into how technical factors influence bias mitigation strategies. By tackling these challenges and suggesting areas for future research, we aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion about gender bias in language technologies, promoting more equitable and inclusive NLP systems.
